items.question: You open DevTools on your production site, type `throw new Error('observability-test')` in the console, and nothing appears in Sentry. Is the SDK broken?
items.answer: No. Code typed into the DevTools console is sandboxed and does not run through your application's error handlers, so it never triggers Sentry's monitoring. Verify from the application itself, for example a button handler or a deliberate verify function that throws, then confirm the issue arrived in the Sentry project with the expected environment and release. Use a clearly labeled test error or a non-production environment so verification cannot pollute real incident data.
items.trap: The naive conclusion is that the SDK or DSN is misconfigured, so people start changing init code. The failure is in the verification method: console-thrown errors never pass through the application's monitoring path, so the test proves nothing about Sentry either way.

items.question: Your team wraps every handler in try/catch and shows a friendly toast, but Sentry shows no issues even though users report failures. Why?
items.answer: Automatic reporting covers uncaught exceptions and unhandled promise rejections. A caught exception is handled as far as the browser is concerned, so nothing propagates to the global handlers the SDK hooks. If a handled error still matters for observability, report it explicitly with captureException, ideally with the operation's context attached.
items.trap: The common assumption is that an error-tracking SDK hooks every throw in the codebase. It only sees errors that reach the global uncaught and unhandledrejection paths, so silent catch blocks make failures invisible to monitoring while users still experience them.

items.question: A developer argues for logging every function call at debug level in production, 'just in case'. Why is one wide, structured event per operation more useful than many thin logs?
items.answer: Debugging needs the state that explains an operation, not a transcript of execution. A single wide event with stable fields such as order_id, item_count, and duration_ms can be filtered, aggregated, and correlated with its trace, error, or replay. Many thin logs create noise and cost, and each line lacks the context to explain anything on its own. Keep debug-level logging out of production when it is not needed.
items.trap: The instinct is that more log lines mean more information. In practice volume destroys signal: thin logs cannot be filtered by stable fields, cannot be correlated, and the one line you need during an incident is buried in noise.

items.question: Your log schema includes a free-form `user_email` attribute and a `notes` field where developers append whatever they want. What have you actually built, and what should change?
items.answer: You have built an uncontrolled data export. Logs can contain high-cardinality user and business data, and free-form fields will eventually carry secrets or personal data. Redact sensitive attributes before transport, define which fields are allowed with stable names, and define ownership and retention for log data separately from the client logging API, because the client API cannot enforce policy by itself.
items.trap: The naive view is that logs are harmless because they are 'just text' and only engineers read them. Once arbitrary attributes leave the browser, retention, access, and privacy become real obligations, and high-cardinality fields also inflate cost and make queries harder.

items.question: Lighthouse reports all-green Core Web Vitals in CI, but field data shows real users failing. Give two concrete mechanisms the lab run structurally cannot see.
items.answer: First, INP requires real user interaction, so lab tools cannot measure it and use TBT as a proxy; interaction-driven slowness only appears in field data. Second, field CLS can include layout shifts well after initial load, such as late images or injected content, which a lab page-load simulation misses. Lab also runs on controlled devices and networks, not the population of real hardware and conditions.
items.trap: The reflex is to distrust one of the two numbers, either 'Lighthouse is wrong' or 'RUM is noisy'. Both are correct answers to different questions: lab is a controlled simulation for development and regression diagnosis, while field data measures what actual users experience on their devices, networks, and interactions.

items.question: A PM asks for 'our average INP' to put in a slide. Why is the average the wrong number, and what do you report instead?
items.answer: Averages hide the tail, and Core Web Vitals are about the proportion of visits having a good experience. Google's recommended passing view is the 75th percentile of field data meeting each metric's good threshold: LCP at or under 2.5 seconds, INP at or under 200 milliseconds, CLS at or under 0.1. Report the distribution and the p75 per metric, segmented by device or cohort when that explains differences.
items.trap: The average can look healthy while a large minority of users have an unacceptable experience, so the slide says 'we pass' while the field data says many users do not. A single average also merges different devices, networks, and routes into a meaningless blend.

items.question: Current-release errors symbolicate fine, but events from a release deployed two weeks ago still show minified frames even though CI 'uploads maps on every build'. What is the most likely explanation?
items.answer: Symbolication depends on the exact artifact that was deployed with that release. Check whether the map for that specific release was generated and uploaded before those errors occurred, whether the upload actually succeeded, and whether the uploaded artifact belongs to the same release or Debug ID as the browser events. Also check whether the generated file was changed after upload, for example by a post-build step, which breaks the association. Sentry's current default injects Debug IDs into build output, so inspect the deployed artifact for the expected association.
items.trap: The naive fix is 'run the upload again' or 'redeploy'. Uploading a new artifact does not repair the association for events that reference a different release, or a generated file that no longer matches what was uploaded. The investigation has to be per-release and per-artifact, not global.

items.question: A teammate proposes hosting the maps publicly at https://app.example.com/assets/app.js.map so the browser can fetch them. Why is that the wrong default, and what is the recommended approach?
items.answer: A publicly hosted source map exposes your original source code to anyone who asks for it, so it should only ever be an intentional security decision, not a debugging convenience. The recommended approach is uploading maps privately to the error service as part of CI, associated with the release or Debug ID, so symbolication works without publishing sources.
items.trap: The common justification is 'source maps are only used by developer tools'. In reality a public URL serves the full original source, comments included, to anyone, and once it is indexed or scraped you cannot un-publish it. Private upload gives the same debugging result without the exposure.

items.question: An 'error rate above 1 percent' alert pages on-call during every deploy, recovers minutes later, and the team has started ignoring it. Raising the threshold is proposed. Why is that the wrong fix, and what is the right one?
items.answer: Raising the threshold hides the signal along with the noise: a real incident above the new threshold is detected later, and the alert still represents nothing anyone decided to act on. Redesign it around the operational decision: who must act, how quickly, and what evidence indicates user or business impact. Scope the source and environment, use filters for severity, ownership, or affected release so a known rollout spike is separated from a new regression, and route the routine signal to a ticket or channel instead of the on-call page. Then measure noise after rollout and remove alerts nobody acts on.
items.trap: The naive theory is that alert fatigue is a threshold-tuning problem. It is a decision problem: an alert should represent a threshold that changes behavior. If nobody can say what action the alert demands, no threshold value fixes it.

items.question: You review a Sentry alert rule with two filter groups, `environment: production` and `release: v2.3.1`. The author says 'obviously both must match'. What do you check before trusting that?
items.answer: The semantics of how the rule combines triggers and filter groups. Sentry supports multiple triggers with an ANY relationship, and filter groups can be combined with ANY or ALL. If the groups are evaluated with ANY, events matching either condition alert, which is wider than the author intended. Make the combination semantics explicit when reviewing the rule instead of assuming AND everywhere.
items.trap: People import AND semantics from general programming and assume that stacking filters narrows an alert. With ANY between triggers or filter groups, adding conditions widens the rule, so the alert fires on populations the author believed were excluded.

items.question: You cannot reproduce the bug locally, so you want to ship a build full of extra console.log statements to catch the next occurrence. What does this do to the investigation?
items.answer: It resets the evidence chain. The new build is a new release, so the telemetry you already correlated (errors, logs, traces, replays tied to the affected release) no longer describes the code users will run, and the bug may not even reproduce on the new build. Preserve evidence first: affected release, environment, route, browser, cohort, and time window, correlated with logs, trace spans, network failures, and replay. Use a safe reproduction path such as feature-flagged diagnostics, a canary, or a synthetic test, and confirm that source maps and sampling have not biased what you are seeing.
items.trap: The instinct is 'more logging will catch it'. In fact the strongest evidence is what you already have from the affected release, and shipping a new build to debug an intermittent bug trades known evidence for a gamble on future evidence.

items.question: The intermittent bug is failing checkouts for a small but growing number of users. Do you investigate first or mitigate first?
items.answer: Mitigate first when impact is high: disable the flag, roll back, or reduce traffic while the telemetry is preserved. Then investigate from the preserved evidence, comparing affected and unaffected cohorts rather than relying on a single report. After the fix, keep a regression signal and an alert tied to the failure mode, not merely the old exception text, so the same user impact cannot silently return.
items.trap: The naive priority is 'find the root cause before touching production, otherwise you destroy the evidence'. The opposite is true: rollback and flags are the documented mitigation path, and preserving telemetry, not freezing the deploy, is what protects the investigation.

items.question: Every service in the path emits spans, but the result is one disconnected trace per service with no shared timeline. The proposal is 'emit more spans'. What is actually missing?
items.answer: Context propagation. Spans belong to one trace only if they share the trace ID and form a parent-child hierarchy, and that context must be carried across process boundaries with the outgoing request, with W3C Trace Context headers as the usual mechanism. Without propagation, each service produces disconnected timing data no matter how many spans it emits. Instrument the boundaries first, then use stable operation names and semantic attributes.
items.trap: The assumption is that span volume builds the trace. Structure does: a trace is assembled from propagated context, so the fix is at the request boundary, injecting and extracting context, not inside the services.

items.question: To control cost, tracing was set to a low uniform sample rate in production. Now the rare slow checkout, the exact case leadership cares about, almost never appears. How should sampling be designed instead?
items.answer: Sample deliberately rather than uniformly: at high traffic keep the base rate low, but preserve enough errors and slow or important business paths to diagnose tail latency, so the sampling policy protects the paths you actually investigate. Also keep attributes bounded: secrets and unbounded high-cardinality values in attributes carry cost and privacy exposure without a clear policy.
items.trap: The naive model is that sampling is a dial between 'cheap' and 'complete'. Uniform sampling silently deletes the rare tail events, which are precisely the highest-value traces, so the cheap setting costs you the answers you bought tracing for.

items.question: `maskAllText` is enabled, yet a replay shows a value that should have been masked on a custom checkout component. What does that tell you, and what do you do?
items.answer: Masking is configured per surface (text, inputs, media, and other sensitive areas), and rules must be validated against your real UI, not assumed. Test the masking configuration with realistic account and checkout flows, extend the masking or blocking rules to the surfaces that leaked, and re-test. Treat the leak as a policy failure, not a one-off: the allowed-data policy defines what may ever be captured.
items.trap: The common belief is that masking is a single switch that, once set, covers the whole page. In practice every custom surface is a case to verify, and a realistic-flow test is the only way to know the rules actually hold.

items.question: A user with an ad blocker reports the exact failure mode you are hunting, but there is no replay and no error event for their session. What is this failure mode, and how do you design around it?
items.answer: Client telemetry has a blind spot: blocking extensions can prevent the SDK from loading or sending, so the users you most need data from can be exactly the ones you cannot see. Design around it by not making replay the only signal: correlate with server-side evidence such as logs, traces, and network failures where available, review the ad-blocker failure mode of your setup, and treat 'no data from this user' as expected rather than as proof the bug did not happen.
items.trap: The naive inference is 'no replay means the user is fine' or 'the report is wrong'. Absence of client telemetry is not absence of the bug; it can mean the telemetry itself was blocked.

items.question: You deploy at 14:00 and the source-map upload step finishes at 14:05. The first error of the new release arrives at 14:02. Why does the ordering matter, and what does it cost you?
items.answer: Artifacts must be available before traffic reaches the new code. The 14:02 event references the deployed artifact, and if the map was not yet uploaded and associated with that release or Debug ID, the first incident of the release is harder to interpret: you are debugging an active issue through minified frames and artifact association instead of reading a symbolicated stack. Sequence CI so the production build's map is generated and uploaded before the deploy exposes the artifact to users.
items.trap: The assumption is that upload order is irrelevant because 'the map will match eventually'. During the first incident of a release, minutes matter, and the events in that window are the ones you most need to read. The fix is pipeline ordering, not faster incident-time debugging.

items.question: You roll back the bad release and the error rate recovers. The incident channel wants to close the incident. What is missing from that reasoning?
items.answer: Rollback is a mitigation, not the investigation. Before closing, preserve the telemetry of the affected release, follow up with an actual fix, and add a regression guard: an alert and a signal tied to the failure mode, not merely the old exception text, plus rollback criteria defined before the next deploy. Otherwise the same change can ship again and the failure returns silently.
items.trap: The naive equation is 'error rate recovered, therefore problem solved'. The user impact was real, the cause is still in the codebase, and without a regression signal the next deploy of that change is indistinguishable from the first time it broke.

items.question: The platform team proposes that the org-wide contract mandate one vendor's SDK in every service, for consistency. Why is that standardizing the wrong layer?
items.answer: The contract should standardize vocabulary and ownership, not implementation detail. Mandating one SDK couples every team's meaning to one backend: when the vendor changes or the org migrates, the semantics go with it. Preserve vendor-neutral concepts (traces, spans, events, logs, metrics) and standardize the fields, naming conventions, severity semantics, sampling and retention rules, and the secrets and personal-data policy, so teams can change backends without losing meaning.
items.trap: The intuition is 'one tool everywhere equals consistent data'. Consistency comes from shared vocabulary and correlation fields, not from a shared SDK; a mandated SDK gives uniformity of implementation while leaving the actual semantics, what an event means and what severity implies, undefined.

items.question: A payments team wants 100 percent trace sampling on a high-volume endpoint because money is on the line. Does the org contract force them to choose between the rule and the debuggability?
items.answer: No. A mature contract includes a documented exception process for high-risk or high-volume instrumentation. The sampling and retention rules are the default, and the exception process defines how a team argues for, reviews, and owns the cost and privacy implications of deviating. The secrets and personal-data policy applies here too, since full sampling of a payments path multiplies sensitive-attribute exposure.
items.trap: The naive reading of a contract is a hard rulebook: either the team silently violates it, or they comply and lose the data they need. The documented exception process is what makes the contract govern high-risk cases instead of pretending they do not exist.

mcqs.question: You need to verify that Sentry is wired up correctly in a production-like environment. Which approach actually tests the complete path?
options: Open DevTools on the deployed site, run `throw new Error('test')` in the console, and wait for the issue to appear.
Confirm that `Sentry.init` runs without warnings during startup and that the bundle contains the SDK.
Trigger a deliberate, clearly labeled error from application code (for example a button handler) and confirm the issue arrives in the Sentry project with the expected environment and release.
Send a test event with the same DSN from a small Node script running on your laptop.
mcqs.explanation: Only an error thrown by the application itself exercises the full path: the SDK's global handlers, the transport, and the release and environment tagging you rely on during incidents. The strongest distractor is the DevTools console: browser-console errors are sandboxed and do not trigger Sentry's monitoring, so that test proves nothing either way. A clean init and a bundled SDK only prove the library loaded, and a Node script tests a different runtime and pipeline, not your users' browser path.

mcqs.question: Which client logging design best matches structured-logging guidance for production?
options: A debug-level log at the top of every function, with debug output enabled in production so nothing is ever missed.
One event per completed operation with stable fields such as `order_id`, `item_count`, and `duration_ms`, at a severity that reflects actionability, with sensitive attributes redacted.
A single free-form message string per event that embeds all the details inline, leaving parsing to whoever reads it later.
Error-level events only, since successful operations carry no diagnostic value.
mcqs.explanation: Guidance favors a wide event with the context needed to explain one operation: stable field names make events filterable and correlatable, and redaction keeps sensitive data in the browser. The strongest distractor is logging every function call: volume destroys signal, thin logs cannot be filtered by stable fields, and debug-level output belongs out of production when it is not needed. Free-form strings and errors-only designs both throw away the correlation and context that make logs useful.

mcqs.question: According to Google's recommended passing view, a page passes Core Web Vitals when which measurement meets the good thresholds?
options: The average of all field loads: LCP at or under 2.5 seconds, INP at or under 200 milliseconds, CLS at or under 0.1.
A Lighthouse lab score of 90 or higher on the reference device in CI.
The median field value per metric, allowing 10 percent of visits to fail without consequence.
The 75th percentile of field (RUM) data: LCP at or under 2.5 seconds, INP at or under 200 milliseconds, CLS at or under 0.1.
mcqs.explanation: The passing view is explicitly the 75th percentile of field data meeting each metric's threshold, because Core Web Vitals measure the proportion of visits with a good experience. The strongest distractor is the average: averages hide the tail, so a healthy average can coexist with many users having an unacceptable experience. Lab scores answer a different, controlled question, and neither averages nor medians express the share of users below the threshold.

mcqs.question: Which statement about lab tools and field data for Core Web Vitals is correct?
options: Lighthouse measures CLS more faithfully than field data because it controls the viewport and device.
Lab tools cannot measure INP because it requires real user interaction, so TBT is used as a lab proxy; field CLS can include shifts after initial load that a lab page load misses.
TBT is a field metric that replaces INP when real-user data is unavailable.
Field data and lab data should always agree; a disagreement means one of the tools is misconfigured.
mcqs.explanation: INP is interaction-driven, so lab runs use TBT as a proxy, and layout shifts that happen after the initial load only show up in field CLS. The strongest distractor is the claim that lab CLS is more faithful: lab runs a controlled simulation, which is exactly why it cannot represent post-load shifts or the diversity of real devices, networks, and locations. Disagreement between lab and field is expected, not a misconfiguration.

mcqs.question: Current-release errors symbolicate correctly, but events from a release deployed two weeks ago still show minified frames. CI says it uploads maps on every build. What should you check first?
options: Whether the exact artifact deployed with that release had its source map generated, successfully uploaded, and associated with the same release or Debug ID before those errors occurred, and whether the generated file was changed after upload.
Whether the source maps need to be hosted publicly next to the JavaScript files so Sentry can fetch them for old releases.
Whether Debug IDs expire once a release is superseded by a newer one.
Whether users' browsers cached the minified file, requiring a cache flush before symbolication works.
mcqs.explanation: Symbolication is per artifact: the event must match the uploaded map for its own release or Debug ID, and a generated file changed after upload breaks the association, so the check is release-specific. The strongest distractor is public hosting: it is a security exposure decision, private upload to the error service is the recommended approach, and it would not explain a release-specific failure anyway. Debug IDs do not expire, and browser caching has nothing to do with server-side artifact association.

mcqs.question: An alert pages on-call during every deploy because the error rate briefly spikes during rollout, then recovers. The team has started ignoring it. What is the best fix?
options: Raise the threshold from 1 percent to 5 percent so deploys stop triggering it.
Delete the alert; error-rate alerts inherently cannot distinguish deploys from incidents.

Redesign the alert around an operational decision: scope it by environment and release, separate a new regression from the known baseline, and route the routine rollout signal to a ticket or channel instead of the page.
Deliver the alert to more channels simultaneously so somebody eventually responds.
mcqs.explanation: Alert fatigue is a decision problem: the alert should represent a threshold that changes behavior, with filters for severity, ownership, or affected release separating expected rollout noise from a new regression. The strongest distractor is raising the threshold: it hides deploy noise and real incidents alike, and detection of genuine regressions gets slower. More channels amplifies noise rather than adding an owner, and the alert is salvageable with scoping, not deletable.

mcqs.question: An intermittent checkout failure affects a small but growing set of production users and cannot be reproduced locally. What is the correct first move?
options: Preserve the evidence (release, environment, cohort, replays, traces), mitigate the impact by disabling a flag, rolling back, or reducing traffic, then investigate by comparing affected and unaffected cohorts.
Ship a build with verbose logging around checkout so the next occurrence is captured in detail.
Wait for a few more weeks of reports so the pattern is statistically solid before changing anything.
Ask the affected users to share their session tokens so you can reproduce their exact state locally.
mcqs.explanation: With high user impact, mitigation comes first (flag, rollback, or traffic reduction) while the telemetry is preserved, and cohort comparison is the investigation method that does not require local reproduction. The strongest distractor is shipping verbose logging: it creates a new release, breaking the correlation of existing evidence to the code users run, and the bug may not even reproduce on the new build. Waiting prolongs user harm, and asking users for secrets is never an acceptable reproduction path.

mcqs.question: Every service along the request path emits spans, but the result is one disconnected trace per service with no shared timeline. What is missing?
options: More spans inside each service, so the backend has enough data points to merge the traces.
Context propagation: the span context must be carried across process boundaries (for example with W3C Trace Context headers) so spans share a trace ID and form a parent-child hierarchy.
A higher sample rate, because dropped spans are what split the trace into pieces.
Stable operation names, which are the mechanism that joins spans into one trace.
mcqs.explanation: A trace is assembled from propagated context: without the trace context traveling with the outgoing request, each service produces disconnected timing data regardless of how many spans it emits. The strongest distractor is the sample rate: sampling decides which traces are kept, not whether the kept ones connect, and the symptom here is per-service disconnection, not missing data. Stable operation names make traces readable and comparable, but they do not join them.

mcqs.question: Which session replay rollout best matches responsible-use guidance?
options: `replaysSessionSampleRate: 1.0` and `replaysOnErrorSampleRate: 1.0`, so every debugging session is available when someone looks for it.
No masking, with access to the replay dashboard restricted to the on-call team instead.
Replay enabled only in staging, since recording production users is never acceptable.

Masking and blocking configured for text, inputs, and media, validated against realistic account and checkout flows, with a low session sample rate, a high error sample rate, and replays linked to errors, traces, and releases.
mcqs.explanation: Replay is sensitive telemetry: masking rules must be tested on real flows, sampling controls cost and exposure while prioritizing sessions with errors, and linking replays to errors, traces, logs, and releases is what makes them useful for debugging. The strongest distractor is sampling everything at 1.0: it maximizes cost, performance impact, and privacy exposure for sessions that will never be watched. Access control alone still records and stores sensitive data, and staging-only replay removes the production debugging value entirely.

mcqs.question: What should an organization-wide observability contract standardize across frontend and backend teams?
options: Vocabulary and ownership: correlation fields (service, environment, release, route, operation), naming conventions, severity semantics, sampling and retention rules, a secrets and personal-data policy, trace context across boundaries, artifact publication in builds, and alert ownership with runbooks.
A single vendor SDK and identical instrumentation code in every service, so all telemetry is uniform.
Dashboards only, since alerting and sampling are team-specific concerns.
Exact log message wording for common scenarios, so searches return consistent results.
mcqs.explanation: The contract standardizes vocabulary and ownership, not implementation detail, and preserves vendor-neutral concepts (traces, spans, events, logs, metrics) so teams can change backends without losing meaning. The strongest distractor is mandating one vendor SDK: it creates uniformity of implementation while leaving the actual semantics undefined, and it couples the org's meaning to one backend. Dashboards without alert ownership abandon the runbook and escalation path, and fixed message wording is brittle where structured fields are what make data queryable.

scenarios.prompt: This team says 'Sentry never worked in production'. Review the setup, explain why their verification failed and what the initialization is missing, then write the corrected entry point and a verification that actually proves the pipeline.
rubric: Identifies console-thrown errors as sandboxed and therefore not a valid verification path.
Moves Sentry.init earlier than application code (module entry, not a deferred callback).
Adds deployment context: environment and release on init.
Verifies from application code with a clearly labeled test error or in a non-production environment.
Confirms the arrived issue carries the expected environment and release before declaring the pipeline healthy.

scenarios.prompt: The team ships this Core Web Vitals collection and reports 'our average INP is 130 ms, so we pass'. Identify what the code does wrong, what the reported number hides, and how you would report field data instead.
scenarios.modelAnswer: Three problems. First, all three metrics are pushed into one array, so the reported 'average' blends LCP (seconds-scale load timing), INP (interaction responsiveness), and CLS (a unitless shift score). The number is physically meaningless, and the 130 ms claim cannot even be about INP alone. Second, even per metric, the average is the wrong summary: Core Web Vitals are evaluated as the share of visits with a good experience, and Google's recommended passing view is the 75th percentile of field data meeting each threshold (LCP at or under 2.5 seconds, INP at or under 200 milliseconds, CLS at or under 0.1). An average of 130 ms is fully compatible with a quarter of users having unacceptable interactions. Third, one aggregate number per pageview discards the distribution and any segmentation, such as device, route, or cohort, that would explain where the bad experiences live. The transport choice, sendBeacon on pagehide, is the reasonable part and should be kept. Fix: report each metric separately with its name, keep per-visit values server-side, evaluate the p75 per metric against the thresholds, and segment by device or route when the distribution is uneven.
rubric: Recognizes that mixing LCP, INP, and CLS values into one average produces a meaningless number.
States the p75-per-metric evaluation against the thresholds (2.5 seconds, 200 milliseconds, 0.1) instead of an average.
Explains why averages hide the tail of bad experiences.
Keeps field-data collection and the sendBeacon transport rather than switching to lab measurement.
Adds segmentation (device, route, cohort) to explain the distribution.

scenarios.prompt: Refactor this production checkout logging so it is useful during incidents without leaking data or creating noise. Explain each change.
rubric: Replaces whole-object dumps with stable, named fields (order_id, item_count, duration_ms).
Removes or redacts personal data such as user.email before transport.
Emits one wide structured event per operation instead of many thin console lines.
Uses severity that reflects actionability, and reports the handled error explicitly so it is not invisible to error tracking.
Mentions correlation (identifiers linking logs to traces, errors, or replays) and retention or ownership as a separate concern.

scenarios.prompt: This span instrumentation was added around checkout. Predict exactly what the trace shows when `createOrder` rejects, and rewrite the function so the span is correct on every path.
rubric: Predicts that the span never ends when createOrder rejects (missing duration or leaked span).
Notes that the exception is not recorded on the span, so the trace cannot explain the failure.
Ends the span in a finally block so every path (success, rejection, synchronous throw) is covered.
Uses recordException or equivalent to attach the error to the span.
Mentions active-span or context usage so child operations attach to the same trace.
